chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abi Abd Allah, from his father, peace be upon them both, who said:

We command our children to perform salat (prayer) when they are five years old, so command your children to perform salat (prayer) when they are seven years old. And we command our children to observe sawm (fasting) when they are seven years old, according to whatever they are able to bear of the day's fast, even if it is until midday, or more than that, or less; then when thirst and hunger overcome them, they break the fast, so that they become accustomed to fasting and are able to bear it. So command your children, when they are nine years old, to observe sawm (fasting) as much of the day's fast as they are able; then when thirst overcomes them, they break the fast.

Thus, the proper approach regarding these reports is that we carry them upon a mode of recommendation, encouragement, and disciplining, while the former is carried upon obligation, so that the reports do not conflict.

key_terms.التَّأْدِيبِ: disciplining, the pedagogical training of children in acts of worship
key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), the ritual prayer children are instructed to begin practicing
key_terms.الصَّوْمِ: sawm (fasting), the act of fasting that children are gradually trained to observe
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابِ: recommendation, indicating a non-obligatory legal understanding
key_terms.الْعَطَشُ: thirst, a limiting factor that allows the child to break the fast
key_terms.الْغَرَثُ: hunger, mentioned alongside thirst as a hardship in fasting
key_terms.الْوُجُوبِ: obligation, the binding legal status contrasted with recommendation
key_terms.صِبْيَانَنَا: our children, referring to young children being trained in worship

ai.seo_question: At what age should children be instructed to pray and fast according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses gradually training children in salat (prayer) and sawm (fasting) according to their age and ability. It also concludes with a juristic reconciliation, explaining that some reports are to be understood as recommendation and discipline rather than obligation, in order to avoid contradiction between narrations.
